claim: Color perception relies on comparisons between adjacent lights.
source: Color perception relies on comparisons between adjacent lights, but how the brain performs these comparisons is poorly understood.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a foundational premise for the study.

claim: Many double-opponent (DO) cells responded to chromatic contrast as a weighted sum, akin to how other V1 neurons responded to luminance contrast.
source: We found that many double-opponent (DO) cells, which have spatially and chromatically opponent RFs, responded to chromatic contrast as a weighted sum, akin to how other V1 neurons responded to luminance contrast.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Some neurons integrated chromatic signals nonlinearly.
source: Yet other neurons integrated chromatic signals nonlinearly, confirming that linear signal integration is not an obligate property of V1 neurons.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental measurements.

claim: Linear signal integration is not an obligate property of V1 neurons.
source: Yet other neurons integrated chromatic signals nonlinearly, confirming that linear signal integration is not an obligate property of V1 neurons.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observation of nonlinear integration in some neurons.

claim: The functional similarity of cone-opponent DO cells and cone non-opponent simple cells suggests that these two groups may share a common underlying circuitry.
source: The functional similarity of cone-opponent DO cells and cone non-opponent simple cells suggests that these two groups may share a common underlying circuitry, promotes the construction of image-computable models for full-color image representation, and sheds new light on V1 complex cells.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional similarity observed in the data.

claim: Color depends on the spectral composition and spatial organization of lights.
source: Color depends on the spectral composition and spatial organization of lights (Brown and MacLeod, 1997; Kraft and Brainard, 1999; Monnier and Shevell, 2003; Shevell and Monnier, 2005; Xian and Shevell, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The joint spectral and spatial statistics of lights in natural scenes are critical for object recognition, visual memory, and scene segmentation.
source: The joint spectral and spatial statistics of lights in natural scenes are critical for object recognition, visual memory, and scene segmentation (Fine et al., 2003; Spence et al., 2006; Wurm et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The spatial integration of spectral signals by neurons in the visual system is poorly understood.
source: Despite its importance for these critical functions, however, the spatial integration of spectral signals by neurons in the visual system is poorly understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Some V1 neurons combine signals from all cone photoreceptor types with the same sign.
source: Some V1 neurons combine signals from all cone photoreceptor types (from which they receive any input at all) with the same sign.
evidence: This is a description of cone non-opponent neurons based on established knowledge.

claim: Many cone non-opponent neurons have receptive fields consisting of side-by-side ON and OFF subfields, rendering them sensitive to luminance contrast of a particular orientation at a particular location in their RFs.
source: Many of these cone non-opponent neurons have receptive fields (RFs) consisting of side-by-side ON and OFF subfields, rendering them sensitive to luminance contrast of a particular orientation at a particular location in their RFs.
evidence: This describes the properties of cone non-opponent neurons based on established knowledge.

claim: Other V1 neurons combine signals from multiple cone types with opposite sign and are therefore cone-opponent.
source: Other V1 neurons combine signals from multiple cone types with opposite sign and are therefore cone-opponent.
evidence: This is a definition of cone-opponent neurons based on established knowledge.

claim: A subset of V1 cone-opponent neurons, called double-opponent (DO) cells, are both cone-opponent and spatially opponent, rendering them sensitive to chromatic edges of particular orientations at particular locations in their RFs.
source: A subset of V1 cone-opponent neurons, called double-opponent (DO) cells, are both cone-opponent and spatially opponent, rendering them sensitive to chromatic edges of particular orientations at particular locations in their RFs (Conway, 2001; De and Horwitz, 2021a; Johnson et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a definition of DO cells supported by citations.

claim: V1 is the first stage of the primate visual system at which DO cells exist.
source: V1 is the first stage of the primate visual system at which DO cells exist (Hubel and Wiesel, 1968; Livingstone and Hubel, 1984).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: V1 is the first stage of the primate visual system that contains simple cells.
source: V1 is also the first stage of the primate visual system that contains simple cells (Hubel and Wiesel, 1968).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Simple cells respond to a drifting achromatic sinusoidal grating of appropriate spatial- and temporal-frequency with spike rate modulation that exceeds the unmodulated response.
source: These cells, by definition, respond to a drifting achromatic sinusoidal grating of appropriate spatial- and temporal-frequency with spike rate modulation that exceeds the unmodulated response (Skottun et al., 1991).
evidence: This is a definition of simple cells supported by a citation.

claim: The definition of simple cells likely includes many DO cells when applied to macaque V1 neurons.
source: Applied to macaque V1 neurons, this definition likely includes many DO cells (simple cells were originally characterized in cat, an animal with few if any cone-opponent V1 neurons).
evidence: This is an inference based on the original characterization of simple cells in cats.

claim: Cone non-opponent simple cells have much in common with DO cells.
source: Cone non-opponent simple cells have much in common with DO cells (De and Horwitz, 2021a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Classically defined simple cells combine light information across their RFs approximately as a weighted sum.
source: Classically defined simple cells combine light information across their RFs approximately as a weighted sum (Carandini et al., 1997; DeAngelis et al., 1993; Hubel and Wiesel, 1959; Movshon et al., 1978b).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Simple cells can be thought of as linear filters that operate on the retinal image.
source: These neurons can therefore be thought of as linear filters that operate on the retinal image.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the linear summation property of simple cells.

claim: The linear filtering property of simple cells facilitated the construction of image-computable models of achromatic image representation.
source: This insight propelled scientific progress in at least three ways. First, it facilitated the construction of image-computable models of achromatic image representation (Adelson and Bergen, 1991; Marr and Hildreth, 1980; Mehrotra et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Simple cells receive excitation (push) and inhibition (pull) with opposite spatial tuning, which is critical for establishing linearity in the face of nonlinear input from the LGN.
source: Second, it shed light on cortical circuitry: simple cells receive excitation (push) and inhibition (pull) with opposite spatial tuning, and this appears to be a critical step for establishing linearity in the face of nonlinear input from the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) (Ferster, 1988; Ferster and Miller, 2000; Hirsch et al., 1998; McLaughlin, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The linear filtering property of simple cells provided an essential building block for quantitative models of V1 complex cells, neurons in higher-order cortical areas, and a variety of psychophysical phenomena.
source: Third, it provided an essential building block for quantitative models of V1 complex cells (Adelson and Bergen, 1985; Movshon et al., 1978a), neurons in higher-order cortical areas (Cadieu et al., 2007; Freeman et al., 2013; Okazawa et al., 2015; Rust et al., 2006; Simoncelli and Heeger, 1998; Willmore et al., 2010), and a variety of psychophysical phenomena (Adelson and Bergen, 1985; Beaudot and Mullen, 2006; Graham, 2011; Malik and Perona, 1990; Moreland and Boynton, 2017; Wilson et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: All of the advances related to linear filtering by simple cells have been restricted to the achromatic domain.
source: Currently, all of these advances have been restricted to the achromatic domain.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of the field.

claim: A similar quantitative understanding of image representation in the chromatic domain is lacking and is necessary to extend these advances to natural, full-color images.
source: A similar quantitative understanding of image representation in the chromatic domain is lacking and is necessary to extend these advances to natural, full-color images.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of the field and the motivation for the study.

claim: If a DO cell integrates signals linearly and with equal weight, then it is well suited for extracting vertical chromatic edges.
source: If the cell integrates signals linearly and with equal weight, then it is well suited for extracting vertical chromatic edges (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: In a linear DO cell, the excitation produced by a preferred light in one half of the RF can be canceled by the same light in the neighboring half.
source: In this case, the excitation produced by a preferred light in one half of the RF can be canceled by the same light in the neighboring half.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction for linear integration.

claim: If a DO cell integrates signals nonlinearly, for example, by weighting contrast increments more heavily than contrast decrements, it would encode both edges and surfaces.
source: On the other hand, if the cell integrates signals nonlinearly, for example, by weighting contrast increments more heavily than contrast decrements, it would encode both edges and surfaces (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: In a nonlinear DO cell, a light in one half of the RF would fail to cancel the same light appearing in the neighboring half.
source: In this case, a light in one half of the RF would fail to cancel the same light appearing in the neighboring half.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction for nonlinear integration.

claim: 98 V1 neurons from two awake, fixating male macaque monkeys were analyzed (69 from Monkey 1, 29 from Monkey 2).
source: We analyzed the spiking responses of 98 V1 neurons from two awake, fixating male macaque monkeys (69 from Monkey 1, 29 from Monkey 2).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental dataset.

claim: Each neuron was visually stimulated with pixel white noise: a 10×10 grid of square, 0.2° pixels, each of which changed randomly and independently on every screen refresh.
source: Each neuron was visually stimulated with pixel white noise: a 10×10 grid of square, 0.2° pixels, each of which changed randomly and independently on every screen refresh.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Data were analyzed by spike-triggered averaging to identify a pair of functionally distinct subfields within the classical RF.
source: Data were analyzed by spike-triggered averaging to identify a pair of functionally distinct subfields within the classical RF.
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis methods.

claim: Spike-triggered averages (STAs) of some neurons resembled uniform blobs, indicating invariant spectral sensitivity across the RF.
source: Spike-triggered averages (STAs) of some neurons resembled uniform blobs, indicating invariant spectral sensitivity across the RF.
evidence: This is an observation from the data.

claim: Other STAs were spatially structured, for example, consisting of a set of yellow pixels adjacent to a set of blue pixels.
source: Other STAs were spatially structured, for example, consisting of a set of yellow pixels adjacent to a set of blue pixels (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is an observation from the data illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: Structured STAs are a signature of neurons that compare spectral information across space.
source: These structured STAs are a signature of neurons that compare spectral information across space.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the structured STAs.

claim: If an STA did not reveal at least two distinct subfields, the neuron was passed over for data collection.
source: If an STA did not reveal at least two distinct subfields, the neuron was passed over for data collection.
evidence: This is a description of the neuron selection criteria.

claim: The two sides of the hyperpixel STAs from simple cells and DO cells were complementary, or nearly so.
source: The two sides of the hyperpixel STAs from simple cells and DO cells were complementary, or nearly so.
evidence: This is an observation from the data.

claim: The complementarity of hyperpixel STAs was evident via a comparison between the background-subtracted red, green, and blue phosphor intensities at the two hyperpixels (Pearson's r=–0.94±0.11 (mean ± SD) for simple cells and –0.76±0.23 for DO cells).
source: This complementarity was evident via a comparison between the background-subtracted red, green, and blue phosphor intensities at the two hyperpixels (Pearson's r=–0.94±0.11 (mean ± SD) for simple cells and –0.76±0.23 for DO cells), and between cone weights derived from these RGB values (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis of the data.

claim: NLIs differed across the three cell types (median white noise NLI for DO cells=0.0005, simple cells=0.0009, OSO cells=0.0034; p=0.02, Kruskal-Wallis test).
source: NLIs differed across the three cell types (median white noise NLI for DO cells=0.0005, simple cells=0.0009, OSO cells=0.0034; p=0.02, Kruskal-Wallis test; Figure 2D–F).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Comparison between simple and DO cells revealed no significant difference in white noise NLIs between them (p=0.99, Mann-Whitney U-test).
source: Comparison between simple and DO cells revealed no significant difference between them (p=0.99, Mann-Whitney U-test).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the data.

claim: NLIs of simple and DO cells were both lower than those of the OSO cells (p<0.05, Mann-Whitney U-test).
source: To the contrary, NLIs of simple and DO cells were both lower than those of the OSO cells (p<0.05, Mann-Whitney U-test).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Neurons classified as simple or DO combined signals across space with a similar degree of linearity and more linearly than other V1 neurons that also had spatially structured STAs.
source: In short, neurons that we classified as simple or DO combined signals across space with a similar degree of linearity and more linearly than other V1 neurons that also had spatially structured STAs.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the white noise analysis.

claim: The isoresponse method is robust to static output nonlinearities.
source: An advantage of this approach is that it is robust to static output nonlinearities.
evidence: This is a statement about the properties of the isoresponse method.

claim: For some neurons, staircase termination points lay close to a line when plotted in the stimulus space.
source: For some neurons, staircase termination points lay close to a line when plotted in the stimulus space (Figure 3A–B & Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an observation from the data illustrated in Figure 3.

claim: Staircase termination points lying close to a line shows that the excitation produced by a preferred light in one part of the RF can be canceled by an anti-preferred light in a neighboring part with a fixed constant of proportionality over the entire gamut of the video display.
source: This result shows that the excitation produced by a preferred light in one part of the RF can be canceled by an anti-preferred light in a neighboring part with a fixed constant of proportionality over the entire gamut of our video display.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the linear staircase termination points.

claim: Staircase termination points lying close to a line is consistent with linearity of spatial integration.
source: This cancelation is consistent with linearity of spatial integration (Figure 1A) and not with differential sensitivity to contrast increments and decrements (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the linear staircase termination points.

claim: For some neurons, staircase termination points lay on a curve, consistent with nonlinear spatial integration.
source: However, not all neurons behaved this way. For some neurons, staircase termination points lay on a curve (Figure 3C), consistent with nonlinear spatial integration.
evidence: This is an observation from the data illustrated in Figure 3C.

claim: Isoresponse NLIs of DO cells and simple cells were close to zero and did not differ significantly (median isoresponse NLI for DO cells=0.1007, median isoresponse NLI for simple cells=–0.0097; p=0.14, Mann-Whitney U-test).
source: Isoresponse NLIs of DO cells and simple cells were close to zero and did not differ significantly (median isoresponse NLI for DO cells=0.1007, median isoresponse NLI for simple cells=–0.0097; p=0.14, Mann-Whitney U-test; Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Isoresponse NLIs were greater for OSO neurons (median isoresponse NLI=0.2822, p=0.02, Kruskal-Wallis test).
source: In contrast, NLIs were greater for OSO neurons (median isoresponse NLI=0.2822, p=0.02, Kruskal-Wallis test).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Neurons classified as simple cells and DO cells are similarly linear over the range tested given the limits of the display.
source: We conclude that neurons that we classified as simple cells and DO cells are similarly linear over the range that we were able to test given the limits of our display and that they are more linear than other neurons in V1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the isoresponse NLI analysis.

claim: Neurons classified as simple cells and DO cells are more linear than other neurons in V1.
source: We conclude that neurons that we classified as simple cells and DO cells are similarly linear over the range that we were able to test given the limits of our display and that they are more linear than other neurons in V1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the isoresponse NLI analysis.

claim: Isoresponse NLIs (from Phase 3) were positively correlated with white noise NLIs (from Phase 2) (r=0.30, p=0.001, Spearman's correlation).
source: Isoresponse NLIs (from Phase 3 of the experiment) were positively correlated with white noise NLIs (from Phase 2 of the experiment) (r=0.30, p=0.001, Spearman's correlation; Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the data.

claim: The correlation between isoresponse NLIs and white noise NLIs was driven primarily by OSO cells (r=0.41, p=0.004) and not by DO (r=0.01, p=0.95) or simple cells (r=–0.19, p=0.34).
source: This correlation was driven primarily by OSO cells (r=0.41, p=0.004,) and not by DO (r=0.01, p=0.95,) or simple cells (r=–0.19, p=0.34).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Within-subfield NLIs differed across the three cell types (p<0.0001, Kruskal-Wallis test).
source: Within-subfield NLIs differed across the three cell types (p<0.0001, Kruskal-Wallis test; Figure 5).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the data.

claim: On average, within-subfield NLIs were higher for OSO cells than for simple or DO cells (median within-subfield NLI for simple cells=–0.0016, for DO cells=–0.0003, for OSO cells=0.0047, p<0.0001, Kruskal-Wallis test).
source: On average, within-subfield NLIs were higher for OSO cells than for simple or DO cells (median within-subfield NLI for simple cells=–0.0016, for DO cells=–0.0003, for OSO cells=0.0047, p<0.0001, Kruskal-Wallis test).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Simple cells and DO cells combine signals with a similar degree of linearity within individual RF subfields.
source: This result extends to individual RF subfields the observation that simple cells and DO cells combine signals with a similar degree of linearity and shows that the nonlinear signal integration exhibited by many OSO cells is poorly described as resulting from a nonlinear combination of two linear RF subfields.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the within-subfield NLI analysis.

claim: The nonlinear signal integration exhibited by many OSO cells is poorly described as resulting from a nonlinear combination of two linear RF subfields.
source: This result extends to individual RF subfields the observation that simple cells and DO cells combine signals with a similar degree of linearity and shows that the nonlinear signal integration exhibited by many OSO cells is poorly described as resulting from a nonlinear combination of two linear RF subfields.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the within-subfield NLI analysis.

claim: Many V1 neurons that are driven strongly by modulations of the S-cones are poorly described by a linear model.
source: Many V1 neurons that are driven strongly by modulations of the S-cones are poorly described by a linear model (Horwitz et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The absolute value of the normalized S-cone weight derived from the hyperpixel STA was correlated with isoresponse NLI (r=0.23, p=0.02, Spearman's correlation).
source: Consistent with this observation, we found that the absolute value of the normalized S-cone weight derived from the hyperpixel STA was correlated with isoresponse NLI (r=0.23, p=0.02, Spearman's correlation; Figure 6).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the data.

claim: S-cone weight did not correlate significantly with white noise NLI or within-subfield NLI (both r<0.2, p>0.05).
source: However, S-cone weight did not correlate significantly with the other two NLIs (white noise and within-subfield, both r<0.2, p>0.05).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Some DO cells integrate signals across their RFs linearly, like cone non-opponent simple cells do and in contrast to other V1 neurons.
source: In this study, we characterized the spatial integration of light by neurons in area V1 of macaques with two types of visual white noise stimulation, closed-loop isoresponse measurements, and statistical model comparisons. We found that some DO cells integrate signals across their RFs linearly, like cone non-opponent simple cells do and in contrast to other V1 neurons.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: The study did not find strong evidence for V1 neurons that pool information linearly across cone photoreceptor types within a subfield and then nonlinearly across subfields.
source: We did not find strong evidence for V1 neurons that pool information linearly across cone photoreceptor types within a subfield and then nonlinearly across subfields.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings regarding within-subfield integration.

claim: The linearity of V1 simple cells is not an accident of random convergence of LGN afferents but rather the product of specialized excitatory and inhibitory circuitry.
source: The linearity of V1 simple cells is not an accident of random convergence of LGN afferents but rather the product of specialized excitatory and inhibitory circuitry (Ferster, 1988; Hirsch et al., 1998; Tolhurst and Dean, 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The discovery that V1 simple cells combine signals linearly across their RFs contributed to scientific progress in many ways.
source: The discovery that V1 simple cells combine signals linearly across their RFs contributed to scientific progress in many ways.
evidence: This is a statement about the historical impact of prior research.

claim: The linear model remains a cornerstone of even nonlinear V1 models.
source: It served as a basis for more elaborate models; all V1 neurons exhibit some degree of nonlinearity, but the linear model remains a cornerstone of even nonlinear V1 models (Carandini, 2006; Carandini et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Nearly all quantitative studies of V1 spatial RF properties have used achromatic stimuli.
source: Nearly all quantitative studies of V1 spatial RF properties have used achromatic stimuli (but see Conway, 2001; Conway et al., 2002; Conway and Livingstone, 2006; Johnson et al., 2001; Johnson et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of the field with citations to exceptions.

claim: Extending quantitative RF mapping to color is complicated by the curse of dimensionality.
source: Extending quantitative RF mapping to color is complicated by the curse of dimensionality.
evidence: This is a statement about the challenges of studying color in V1.

claim: As the dimensionality of the color space increases from 1-D (achromatic) to 3-D (full color), the number of possible spatial combinations grows exponentially.
source: As the dimensionality of the color space increases from 1-D (achromatic) to 3-D (full color), the number of possible spatial combinations grows exponentially.
evidence: This is an explanation of the curse of dimensionality in the context of color vision.

claim: Conway, 2001 found that most color-sensitive V1 neurons responded maximally when a pair of bars that modulated different cone types appeared side-by-side within the RF.
source: Using the 2-bar interaction technique, Conway, 2001 found that most color-sensitive V1 neurons responded maximally when a pair of bars that modulated different cone types appeared side-by-side within the RF.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The maximal response to side-by-side bars exceeded the response to either bar in isolation, consistent with linearity of spatial summation as well other models.
source: This maximal response exceeded the response to either bar in isolation, consistent with linearity of spatial summation as well other models (e.g., those that include an expansive nonlinearity after linear spatial summation).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings from Conway, 2001.

claim: At least one cell was found to integrate signals nonlinearly by Conway, 2001.
source: At least one cell was found to integrate signals nonlinearly (Conway, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Conway and Livingstone, 2006 measured the responses of DO cells to cone-isolating stimuli at individual RF locations.
source: Conway and Livingstone, 2006 measured the responses of DO cells to cone-isolating stimuli at individual RF locations.
evidence: This is a description of prior work.

claim: Most of the DO cells studied by Conway and Livingstone, 2006 showed clear signs of push-pull inhibition, which is correlated with linearity in V1.
source: Most of the DO cells they studied showed clear signs of push-pull inhibition, which is correlated with linearity in V1 (Ferster, 1994; Ferster and Miller, 2000; Hirsch et al., 1998; Tolhurst and Dean, 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The findings of this study extend the results of Conway and Livingstone, 2006 by demonstrating the linearity of spatial integration directly through simultaneous stimulation of functionally distinct RF subfields.
source: Our findings extend these results by demonstrating the linearity of spatial integration directly through simultaneous stimulation of functionally distinct RF subfields.
evidence: This is a statement about how the current study extends prior work.

claim: Most other recent studies of DO cells used cone-isolating stimuli and limited mixtures of those stimuli, which cannot completely reveal interactions among cone types.
source: Most other recent studies of DO cells used cone-isolating stimuli and limited mixtures of those stimuli, which cannot completely reveal interactions among cone types (Conway, 2001; Johnson et al., 2001, Johnson et al., 2004; Conway and Livingstone, 2006; Johnson et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a critique of prior work supported by citations.

claim: The current study used a stimulus set that modulated all three cone types together in a variety of proportions.
source: In contrast, we used a stimulus set that modulated all three cone types together in a variety of proportions.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: The current study stimulated DO cells with colored edges to confirm the spatial and spectral sensitivity inferred from the STAs.
source: In further distinction from other studies, we stimulated DO cells with colored edges to confirm the spatial and spectral sensitivity inferred from the STAs.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Neurons were classified as OSO if their hyperpixel STAs indicated spatial opponency and the first principal component (PC1) of hyperpixel white noise stimuli preceding spikes was larger than expected by chance.
source: We classified neurons as OSO (other spatially opponent) if their hyperpixel STAs indicated spatial opponency and the first principal component (PC1) of hyperpixel white noise stimuli preceding spikes (PC1) was larger than expected by chance.
evidence: This is a description of the cell classification criteria.

claim: The PC1 criterion was necessary to satisfy the assumptions underlying the conversion of the STA to cone weights.
source: This latter criterion was necessary to satisfy the assumptions underlying the conversion of the STA to cone weights, and it ensured that the neurons surviving this filter did not exhibit full-wave rectified responses, which would be inconsistent with the classical definitions of simple cells and DO cells.
evidence: This is an explanation of the rationale for the PC1 criterion.

claim: The PC1 criterion ensured that the neurons surviving this filter did not exhibit full-wave rectified responses, which would be inconsistent with the classical definitions of simple cells and DO cells.
source: This latter criterion was necessary to satisfy the assumptions underlying the conversion of the STA to cone weights, and it ensured that the neurons surviving this filter did not exhibit full-wave rectified responses, which would be inconsistent with the classical definitions of simple cells and DO cells.
evidence: This is an explanation of the rationale for the PC1 criterion.

claim: DO cells and at least some OSO cells may lie on a continuum.
source: Indeed, we suspect that DO cells and at least some OSO cells lie on a continuum.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the data.

claim: Neurons in both DO and OSO categories compare cone-opponent (and possibly non-opponent) signals across space and may comprise multiple distinct subtypes.
source: Neurons in both categories compare cone-opponent (and possibly non-opponent) signals across space and may comprise multiple distinct subtypes.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the data.

claim: Some OSO cells had small NLIs, which is consistent with linear spatial integration.
source: We further note that some OSO cells had small NLIs, which is consistent with linear spatial integration, and some DO cells had large NLIs, consistent with nonlinear integration.
evidence: This is an observation from the data.

claim: Some DO cells had large NLIs, consistent with nonlinear integration.
source: We further note that some OSO cells had small NLIs, which is consistent with linear spatial integration, and some DO cells had large NLIs, consistent with nonlinear integration.
evidence: This is an observation from the data.

claim: The lack of a clear distinction between DO and OSO cell types could be related to the fact that the PC1 and NLI are sensitive to overlapping but distinct types of nonlinearity.
source: This lack of a clear distinction between these cell types could be related to the fact that the PC1 and NLI are sensitive to overlapping but distinct types of nonlinearity, these measures depend on the number of spikes in different ways (the PC1 criterion was based on a statistical test, and the NLI was not), and nonlinearities that are clear with high-contrast, long-duration stimuli are not always detectable with white noise (Tanabe and Cumming, 2008).
evidence: This is a speculation about the reasons for the lack of clear distinction between cell types.

claim: Some cells that were classified as OSO would likely have been classified as DO in other studies.
source: Some cells that we classified as OSO would likely have been classified as DO in other studies (e.g., Conway and Livingstone, 2006; Johnson et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a statement about the differences in classification criteria across studies.

claim: Neurons were found with STAs consistent with a DO classification but PC1s consistent with a complex cell classification.
source: In our study, as in a previous one, neurons were found with STAs consistent with a DO classification but PC1s consistent with a complex cell classification (Horwitz et al., 2007).
evidence: This is an observation from the data supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: A major finding of this study is that a population of DO cells combines cone-opponent signals across their RFs approximately as linearly as simple cells combine non-opponent signals.
source: In any case, a major finding of this study is that a population of DO cells combines cone-opponent signals across their RFs approximately as linearly as simple cells combine non-opponent signals, a result that stands despite the existence of other V1 cells that integrate signals nonlinearly.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: The monkeys made small eye movements that moved the stimuli relative to the RF.
source: The monkeys, although rewarded for fixating, made small eye movements that moved the stimuli relative to the RF.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental conditions.

claim: Eye movements blurred STAs and inflated PC1s (for cells with spatially opponent RFs), but these effects were modest because the eye movements were small relative to the stimulus elements.
source: These eye movements blurred STAs and inflated PC1s (for cells with spatially opponent RFs), but these effects were modest because the eye movements were small relative to the stimulus elements.
evidence: This is an assessment of the impact of eye movements on the data.

claim: Across experiments, the average standard deviation of horizontal and vertical eye positions (including measurement error) was 0.13°, and the largest standard deviation across all experiments was 0.18°.
source: Across experiments, the average standard deviation of horizontal and vertical eye positions (including measurement error) was 0.13°, and the largest standard deviation across all experiments was 0.18° (for reference, the size of each pixel in Phase 1 was 0.2°).
evidence: This is a quantitative description of eye movements.

claim: Neither the horizontal nor vertical standard deviation of eye position varied significantly across cell category (Kruskal-Wallis tests, p<0.1).
source: Importantly for the conclusions of this study, neither the horizontal (H) nor vertical (V) standard deviation varied significantly across cell category (Kruskal-Wallis tests, p<0.1) or correlated with isoresponse NLI (Spearman rank correlation coefficients, r=–0.03 (H), –0.18 (V), p>0.05).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of eye movement data.

claim: Eye position standard deviation did not correlate with isoresponse NLI (Spearman rank correlation coefficients, r=–0.03 (H), –0.18 (V), p>0.05).
source: Importantly for the conclusions of this study, neither the horizontal (H) nor vertical (V) standard deviation varied significantly across cell category (Kruskal-Wallis tests, p<0.1) or correlated with isoresponse NLI (Spearman rank correlation coefficients, r=–0.03 (H), –0.18 (V), p>0.05).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of eye movement data.

claim: Eye movements are unlikely to have contributed substantively to the main conclusions of this study.
source: We conclude that eye movements affected the measurements but are unlikely to have contributed substantively to the main conclusions of this study.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the analysis of eye movement data.

claim: The spectral sensitivity of a V1 neuron is determined by the spectral sensitivity of its excitatory and inhibitory afferents.
source: The spectral sensitivity of a V1 neuron is determined by the spectral sensitivity of its excitatory and inhibitory afferents.
evidence: This is a statement about the neural circuitry underlying V1 neurons.

claim: A cell that is excited by L-ON and M-ON afferents in one part of its RF, and by L-OFF and M-OFF afferents in another, is spatially opponent but not cone-opponent.
source: A cell that is excited by L-ON and M-ON afferents in one part of its RF, and by L-OFF and M-OFF afferents in another, is spatially opponent but not cone-opponent.
evidence: This is a description of a hypothetical neuron.

claim: Spatial linearity in a spatially opponent but not cone-opponent cell could be implemented via spectrally matched push-pull inhibition.
source: Spatial linearity in such a cell could be implemented via spectrally matched push-pull inhibition: L-OFF and M-OFF inhibition from the ON subfield and L-ON and M-ON inhibition from the OFF subfield.
evidence: This is a speculation about the neural circuitry underlying spatial linearity.

claim: Pooling the same afferent signals to produce cone-opponency with otherwise identical circuitry would produce a linear L-M DO cell.
source: Pooling the same afferent signals to produce cone-opponency (e.g., pairing L-OFF with M-ON and L-ON with M-OFF) with otherwise identical circuitry would produce a linear L-M DO cell.
evidence: This is a speculation about the neural circuitry underlying linear DO cells.

claim: S-cone signals, which are prevalent in DO cells and, to a lesser degree in simple cells, defy the simple explanation of spectrally matched push-pull inhibition.
source: S-cone signals, which are prevalent in DO cells and, to a lesser degree in simple cells, defy this simple explanation.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the proposed circuitry model.

claim: S-cone ON and OFF pathways in the retina and LGN are highly asymmetric with regard to the L- and M-cone signals they carry.
source: S-cone ON and OFF pathways in the retina and LGN are highly asymmetric with regard to the L- and M-cone signals they carry (Tailby et al., 2008; Wool et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The asymmetries in S-cone pathways may contribute to the nonlinearity of S-cone-dominated V1 neurons.
source: One possibility is that these asymmetries contribute to the nonlinearity of S-cone-dominated V1 neurons.
evidence: This is a speculation about the relationship between S-cone pathway asymmetries and nonlinearity.

claim: Simple cells are thought to provide the dominant input to complex cells.
source: Simple cells are thought to provide the dominant input to complex cells (Alonso and Martinez, 1998; Hubel and Wiesel, 1962).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Under a standard model, complex cells pool signals from simple cells with overlapping RFs and shared preferred orientation.
source: Under a standard model, complex cells pool signals from simple cells with overlapping RFs and shared preferred orientation (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a description of a standard model illustrated in Figure 7A.

claim: Some complex cells may also receive input from DO cells.
source: One possibility is that some complex cells also receive input from DO cells (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a speculation illustrated in Figure 7B.

claim: Complex cells receiving (cone non-opponent) simple cell input only are luminance-sensitive.
source: We speculate that complex cells receiving (cone non-opponent) simple cell input only are luminance-sensitive (Figure 7C) whereas those that receive input from simple and DO cells are both color- and luminance-sensitive (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a speculation illustrated in Figure 7C.

claim: Complex cells that receive input from simple and DO cells are both color- and luminance-sensitive.
source: We speculate that complex cells receiving (cone non-opponent) simple cell input only are luminance-sensitive (Figure 7C) whereas those that receive input from simple and DO cells are both color- and luminance-sensitive (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a speculation illustrated in Figure 7D.

claim: The conjecture that some complex cells receive input from DO cells is consistent with the observation that the preferred orientation of color-sensitive complex cells is maintained across color directions.
source: This conjecture is consistent with the observation that the preferred orientation of color-sensitive complex cells is maintained across color directions (Johnson et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a statement about the consistency of the speculation with prior observations.

claim: The conjecture that some complex cells receive input from DO cells is consistent with the observation that color-sensitive complex cells have multiple preferred color directions by STC analysis.
source: It is also consistent with the observation that color-sensitive complex cells have multiple preferred color directions by STC analysis (Horwitz et al., 2007) and no null directions in cone-contrast space (Horwitz and Hass, 2012).
evidence: This is a statement about the consistency of the speculation with prior observations.

claim: Color-sensitive complex cells have no null directions in cone-contrast space.
source: It is also consistent with the observation that color-sensitive complex cells have multiple preferred color directions by STC analysis (Horwitz et al., 2007) and no null directions in cone-contrast space (Horwitz and Hass, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Complex cells that are insensitive to chromatic modulation abound.
source: Complex cells that are insensitive to chromatic modulation abound (e.g., Figure 7C), whereas those that are insensitive to luminance modulation are exceedingly rare, if present (Horwitz et al., 2007).
evidence: This is an observation from the data and prior work.

claim: Complex cells that are insensitive to luminance modulation are exceedingly rare, if present.
source: Complex cells that are insensitive to chromatic modulation abound (e.g., Figure 7C), whereas those that are insensitive to luminance modulation are exceedingly rare, if present (Horwitz et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The chromatic sensitivity of color-sensitive complex cells could arise entirely from DO cell inputs.
source: Alternatively, the chromatic sensitivity of color-sensitive complex cells could arise entirely from DO cell inputs (Michael, 1978), which have been reported to be similarly responsive to chromatic and luminance contrast (Johnson et al., 2001; Johnson et al., 2004; Johnson et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an alternative speculation supported by citations.

claim: DO cells have been reported to be similarly responsive to chromatic and luminance contrast.
source: Alternatively, the chromatic sensitivity of color-sensitive complex cells could arise entirely from DO cell inputs (Michael, 1978), which have been reported to be similarly responsive to chromatic and luminance contrast (Johnson et al., 2001; Johnson et al., 2004; Johnson et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The chromatic sensitivity of color-sensitive complex cells could arise directly from LGN inputs.
source: Yet another possibility is that it arises directly from LGN inputs.
evidence: This is an alternative speculation.

claim: The explanation that chromatic sensitivity arises directly from LGN inputs is consistent with the direct koniocellular projections to the cytochrome oxidase blobs in area V1.
source: This explanation is consistent with the direct koniocellular projections to the cytochrome oxidase blobs in area V1 (Xiao, 2014), but is difficult to reconcile with the sharp orientation tuning and spatial phase-invariance of some color-sensitive complex cells across color directions.
evidence: This is a statement about the consistency of the speculation with prior observations.

claim: The explanation that chromatic sensitivity arises directly from LGN inputs is difficult to reconcile with the sharp orientation tuning and spatial phase-invariance of some color-sensitive complex cells across color directions.
source: This explanation is consistent with the direct koniocellular projections to the cytochrome oxidase blobs in area V1 (Xiao, 2014), but is difficult to reconcile with the sharp orientation tuning and spatial phase-invariance of some color-sensitive complex cells across color directions.
evidence: This is a statement about the inconsistency of the speculation with prior observations.

claim: The sharp orientation tuning and spatial phase-invariance of some color-sensitive complex cells would seem to require a phase- and orientation-selective upstream intermediate or else elaborate dendritic computations.
source: These visual tuning properties would seem to require a phase- and orientation-selective upstream intermediate or else elaborate dendritic computations.
evidence: This is an inference about the neural mechanisms required to produce observed properties.

claim: The stereotyped microcircuitry of area V1 contributes to vision for form, color, depth, and motion.
source: The stereotyped microcircuitry of area V1 contributes to vision for form, color, depth, and motion.
evidence: This is a statement about the functional role of V1 microcircuitry.

claim: V1 circuits may contribute to distinct visual modalities via a small set of operations that process different signals in similar ways.
source: These distinct visual modalities have distinct computational demands, but V1 circuits may contribute to each via a small set of operations that process different signals in similar ways.
evidence: This is a speculation about the computational principles of V1.

claim: Parallels in the processing of binocular disparity and motion direction in V1 are well established.
source: Parallels in the processing of binocular disparity and motion direction in V1 are well established (Adelson and Bergen, 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Color and stereopsis have heretofore unappreciated parallels.
source: We speculate that color and stereopsis have heretofore unappreciated parallels and that models of binocular disparity tuning may provide a useful guide for the study of cone-opponent and non-opponent signal combinations in V1.
evidence: This is a speculation about parallels between color and stereopsis.

claim: Models of binocular disparity tuning may provide a useful guide for the study of cone-opponent and non-opponent signal combinations in V1.
source: We speculate that color and stereopsis have heretofore unappreciated parallels and that models of binocular disparity tuning may provide a useful guide for the study of cone-opponent and non-opponent signal combinations in V1.
evidence: This is a speculation about the utility of binocular disparity models for studying color.

claim: A fundamental component of binocular V1 models are simple cells that linearly sum signals from the two eyes.
source: A fundamental component of binocular V1 models are simple cells that linearly sum signals from the two eyes (Anzai et al., 1999; Ohzawa and Freeman, 1986; Read and Cumming, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Analogous building blocks in the color domain are simple cells and DO cells that sum cone non-opponent and cone-opponent signals with a similar degree of linearity.
source: Analogous building blocks in the color domain are simple cells and DO cells that sum cone non-opponent and cone-opponent signals with a similar degree of linearity.
evidence: This is a speculation about the analogy between binocular and color processing.

claim: Binocular simple cells are thought to provide input to binocular complex cells that implement a binocular energy calculation.
source: Binocular simple cells are thought to provide input to binocular complex cells that implement a binocular energy calculation (Read and Cumming, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: An analogous convergence of simple cell and DO cell outputs would implement a color energy calculation.
source: An analogous convergence of simple cell and DO cell outputs would implement a color energy calculation (Barnett et al., 2021; Horwitz and Hass, 2012).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citations.

claim: The binocular energy model fails to account for the attenuation of responses to anti-correlated signals between the two eyes.
source: The binocular energy model, while extremely successful in describing complex cell responses, fails to account for the attenuation of responses to anti-correlated signals between the two eyes (Cumming and Parker, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The specialization of real V1 cells for binocularly correlated patterns is thought to reflect the statistics of natural inputs to the visual system.
source: This specialization of real V1 cells is thought to reflect the statistics of natural inputs to the visual system (Haefner and Cumming, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Under natural viewing conditions, binocularly correlated patterns are more common than anti-correlated patterns, and V1 neurons are specialized to encode them.
source: Under natural viewing conditions, binocularly correlated patterns are more common than anti-correlated patterns, and V1 neurons are specialized to encode them.
evidence: This is a statement about the relationship between natural statistics and neural specialization.

claim: A parallel phenomenon may exist in the domain of color.
source: A parallel phenomenon may exist in the domain of color.
evidence: This is a speculation about parallels between binocular and color processing.

claim: Under natural viewing conditions, luminance and chromatic spatial gradients tend to be aligned.
source: Under natural viewing conditions, luminance and chromatic spatial gradients tend to be aligned, and their alignment (or misalignment) carries important information regarding the physical sources of the gradients.
evidence: This is a statement about the statistics of natural images.

claim: The alignment (or misalignment) of luminance and chromatic spatial gradients carries important information regarding the physical sources of the gradients.
source: Under natural viewing conditions, luminance and chromatic spatial gradients tend to be aligned, and their alignment (or misalignment) carries important information regarding the physical sources of the gradients.
evidence: This is a statement about the information content of natural images.

claim: Edges between different materials under fixed illumination produce in-phase luminance and chromatic modulations.
source: Edges between different materials under fixed illumination produce in-phase luminance and chromatic modulations, whereas uncorrelated variations in illumination and pigmentation, such as produced by curved three-dimensional objects of non-uniform reflectance, produce out-of-phase modulations (Cavanagh, 1991; Kingdom, 2003; Kunsberg et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Uncorrelated variations in illumination and pigmentation, such as produced by curved three-dimensional objects of non-uniform reflectance, produce out-of-phase luminance and chromatic modulations.
source: Edges between different materials under fixed illumination produce in-phase luminance and chromatic modulations, whereas uncorrelated variations in illumination and pigmentation, such as produced by curved three-dimensional objects of non-uniform reflectance, produce out-of-phase modulations (Cavanagh, 1991; Kingdom, 2003; Kunsberg et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The energy model produces phase-invariant responses and so does not account for specializations related to natural alignments between chromatic and luminance modulations.
source: The energy model produces phase-invariant responses and so does not account for these specializations.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the energy model.

claim: Whether real V1 neurons respond in accordance with the energy model or show enhanced responses to natural alignments between chromatic and luminance modulations is an important and unanswered question.
source: Whether real V1 neurons respond in accordance with the energy model or show enhanced responses to natural alignments between chromatic and luminance modulations is an important and unanswered question.
evidence: This is a statement about an open question in the field.
